name: Whole-food / unprocessed diet

card.summary: Cutting ultra-processed food in favour of minimally processed eating; observational links to health outcomes, no appearance trials.
card.note: The ultra-processed food concept is debated; appearance effects are untested.

quick.overview:
A whole-food or unprocessed diet avoids ultra-processed products in favour of foods close to their natural form. Appearance-focused communities adopt it for skin, leanness and facial puffiness.

Observational studies link high ultra-processed food intake with obesity and several diseases, but the category is debated and no study has tested appearance outcomes of cutting it.
quick.mechanism: The NOVA classification groups foods by degree of industrial processing. Proposed links to outcomes include energy density, additives and eating patterns, though reference material says mechanisms are unclear.
quick.risks: No notable harms are documented for eating whole foods; critics of the UPF concept note some processed foods are nutritious and that broad condemnation may be oversimplified.

lead: A whole-food or unprocessed diet is built around foods that are close to their natural state, such as vegetables, fruit, grains, legumes, nuts, seeds, unprocessed meat and fish, and limits ultra-processed foods. People adopt it to get leaner, to feel better and to improve how their skin and face look, including less puffiness. Wikipedia defines a whole food as one minimally changed from its natural state that retains a range of nutrients [2].

The reasoning in appearance communities runs through body composition and skin. Supporters say whole foods make staying lean easier, and a leaner face shows the jaw and cheekbones more clearly. An inpatient randomised crossover trial in 20 weight-stable adults compared ultra-processed and unprocessed diets matched for presented calories, energy density, macronutrients, sugar and sodium, and reported in its title that the ultra-processed diet led to excess calorie intake and weight gain [3].

Ultra-processed food (UPF) is defined by the NOVA classification, proposed by Carlos Monteiro and colleagues at the University of São Paulo in 2009 and 2010 [1]. Observational meta-analyses link higher UPF intake with type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease and mortality, while critics say the concept is poorly defined and the evidence largely observational [1]. No study was found on how cutting UPFs affects facial or skin appearance.

General health, leanness, skin and face appearance

paras: NOVA sorts foods by degree of processing rather than nutrient content. UPFs are industrial formulations with many ingredients, often containing sugars, oils, salt and additives rarely used in home cooking [1]. In 2018 the Pan American Health Organization adopted NOVA, which places unprocessed or minimally processed foods in Group 1 [2]. Whole-food diets reduce UPFs in favour of items in that group. Wikipedia uses the Mediterranean diet as its main example of a minimally processed eating pattern and says studies suggest possible associations with lower cardiovascular, childhood obesity and metabolic syndrome risk [2].

sections.h: How it is used for appearance
paras: Appearance-focused communities adopt whole-food eating as a baseline habit for leanness, skin and facial puffiness. The chain is mostly indirect: calorie intake and body fat shape how defined the face looks, and diet quality is said by proponents to influence skin. The Wikipedia article on UPFs proposes that high palatability, low fibre and protein, and a high glycaemic index may promote overeating, although it says the mechanisms are not clear [1].

A 2023 meta-analysis linked each 10 percent increase in UPF intake with about 12 percent higher type 2 diabetes risk, a 2024 meta-analysis found about 17 percent higher cardiovascular risk at the highest versus lowest intake, and a 2025 meta-analysis found about 15 percent higher all-cause mortality [1]. A 2024 BMJ umbrella review noted heterogeneity and unclear mechanisms [1].

Randomised trials of whole-food diets have been run for other outcomes: a whole-food diet for mild to moderate Crohn's disease in children and young adults [5], a whole-food plant-based lifestyle intervention in type 2 diabetes [6], a whole-food plant-based diet in metastatic breast cancer measuring weight and hormonal outcomes [7], and the community-based BROAD study in obesity, ischaemic heart disease and diabetes [8].

Critics argue the UPF term is poorly defined and does not assess nutrient content or amount eaten. In a 2022 debate, Arne Astrup argued NOVA misclassifies foods and relies on observational data, while Monteiro argued associations are consistent and mechanisms plausible; both agreed more research is needed [1]. The UK Scientific Advisory Committee on Nutrition recommended further research, while several Latin American countries recommend avoiding UPFs [1].

No studies found on appearance outcomes. The 2019 NIH inpatient crossover trial compared ultra-processed and unprocessed diets for two weeks each in 20 adults [3]. Wikipedia notes that clinical trial evidence on UPFs and weight is limited and that the often-cited trial has been criticised for not controlling macronutrient profile and energy density [1].

timeline.event: Monteiro and colleagues propose the NOVA framework; formal publication in 2010 [1]
Pan American Health Organization adopts NOVA classification [2]
NIH inpatient randomised trial compares ultra-processed and unprocessed diets [3]

lore.intro: Whole-food eating appears in skin, face-fat and general health threads as a baseline habit.

claims.claim: Cutting ultra-processed food improves skin and reduces facial bloating.
claims.believers: Users report clearer skin and less puffiness after dropping processed food.
claims.experts: Observational studies link UPFs with health outcomes [1]; no study tested skin or facial appearance.

The NIH inpatient trial reported higher calorie intake and weight gain on an ultra-processed diet [3]; Wikipedia says epidemiological links to obesity have not yet been confirmed by randomised trials and the trial has been criticised for not controlling energy density [1].

chain: Meals are filling and lower in added sugar, oils and additives
Easier to stay lean; proponents report clearer skin and less puffiness
angle.text: The diet works mainly through body composition: replacing ultra-processed products with whole foods changes calorie intake and food quality, and people report a leaner face and clearer skin. Skin and puffiness effects are what proponents describe.
